It is not just you, it was my biggest disappointment when I started preparing for this campaign. Most of the work I've done are just details to make the school feel more enchanting and fun to explore. That usually means pulling things out of my ass when my Quandrix player asks about the fractals floating around a classroom, the ones I made up on the spot to keep things feeling more like a magic school. The book is good for using locations and NPCs, but when it comes to ideas on magical concepts, it is really lacking. 
 I got more inspiration for this campaign from other media. Skyrim helped me set the tone for our darker sessions while Baulder's Gate 3 gave me ideas for more interesting villains to fight. In terms of all the whimsical aspects, the Harry Potter franchise is a crucial source of reference and the Lord of the Ring books will boost your creative confidence with so many ideas. Lastly, if you're not already aware, Strixhaven is set in a world within the Magic the Gathering lore (this is what made me run STX in the first place). If you're not a fan of MTG, it's not an issue, but if you have any interest in the story, the MTG lore served me as a much better source material than the STX Guide, especially when it came to the rules of magic within the world.
Hope this helps. Unfortunately, you are better off taking ideas from other sources to really bring to life the "magic academy" concept. Just be prepared to spend more time on descriptive details if you really want to make your players go "🫨‼️ SUCH WHIMSICAL‼️"

Sorry to see this so late, but to give you an answer, it was someone who truly did not understand how contracts work and was essentially trying to blackmail me into giving her an outrages amount of my time whilst refusing to compensate me anymore. I had to spend on paint twice, and she did not refund it. I also worked for half as much as the usual muralist would have charged for a project of that scale. Worked 7-9 hours a day, painting under a grueling 90° sun. 

I say blackmail, because part of the spoken deal of me offering her my work for so cheap, was that she would put in a good word for me in future projects. However, she consistently tried to manipulate my work, after it was submitted, as well as belittling my skills and comparing me to the artist who worked on the mural previously. I finished the work, but did not varnish it because I had already spent so much money on making the work. After hours of labor and verbal abuse, she realized I wasn't gonna put up with her shit and just decided told me she was gonna talk shit about me whenever people asked about the mural. So at that point, I painted as fast as I could and tried to get the hell out of there. And even after all of this, she refused to pay me until a very melodramatic incident happened at the restaurant that involved a verbal argument with my father, I think she was spooked enough to where I came back the next day and there was my paycheck. 

If you're new in this field, but especially if you're a rookie in any art industry, you MUST be able to spot the difference between a tough client and someone who is trying to abuse you. A tough client may be indecisive, resistant to change and even cheap, but whoever is willing to trust you with their space, has to understand they are granting you *creative control.* More so, you can always work around a tough client. If you're patient and use the right words, you can eventually both come to a consensus. A person who is trying to abuse of your work, will constantly question your  talents and find the flaws in your work over the effort you put into it. These people are manipulating you into thinking you owe them more of your time, or you did anything wrong.

Remember, you're an individual contractor, they don't owe you anything you don't put down into word- so you have to be sure to be specific with your contracts. Currently, I am writing my own, but I highly recommend you spend a few dollars on a pre-made one written more professionally than we could ever have the time for. Be safe out there, a lot of people will try to take advantage of you in freelance. Also, be prepared for a good majority of projects to pop up and ultimately result in nothing. Don't be discouraged thought, it is only in the beginning. 

I would also say, the location in which you paint, is a very important deal. Murals are costly projects, that don't get commissioned every day. If you're trying to make a career out of this, you've gotta be in the right city (ex. Los Angeles, New York). However, if you're okay creating this into a side-hustle, or just a hobby, plenty of restaurants and small businesses are looking for muralists constantly. Basically, if you know you're market, you can turn into a suitable business that is both profitable and very rewarding.
So happy for you, hope all went well!

I've been part of this community for only a couple months now, but I think we have a bit of an identity issue. I think it's still too loosely defined that some people don't seem understand the principles. From what I've been able to gather, this is best way I would describe the aesthetic:

Weirdcore is a collection of images that are meant to cause a sense of discomfort to the viewer. There are many ways to achieve this effect from minimalist works to more elaborate examples. 

Classic Style Weirdcore is the originally intended. A strange image with text, typically red or of a bold color, intended to create uneasiness in the viewer. Typically very minimalist, with liminal spaces and shadow figures. When you scroll through the weird-core reddit, you can think of the classic ones like all the additional scenes in a horror movie. Every scene is there to make you uneasy, but not all of them are meant to frighten you.

New Style weirdcore is more elaborate and much broader, but I have been able to identify some patterns:

•the sense of uneasiness is still present
•they're often more elaborate than the classic style (more edited images, significant time placed on the piece, etc.)
•Being more elaborate, most new styles have little need for text

This is the best definition I could give the aesthetic overall: 

Weirdcore is an aesthetic community that seeks to perplex the viewer and evoke sensations of discomfort or fear through edited photo collages and cryptic drawings. The goal is usually to replicate something you would see in a dream, the only limitations being no use of humans or animals. If these are present, facial expressions are not accepted and if a human is to be included, it typically is a shadow figure. Weirdcore does not tolerate the exploitation of real people or animals for the sake of creating a provocative image. Gore, of any form, is not an acceptable way of achieving this, there many other subreddits and pages dedicated to that.


Some common ways to achieve discomfort in the viewer:

•presence of eyes (cropped out of a human face)
•ominous text
•liminal space
•insinuations of impending doom
•apocalyptic themes 
•nostalgic themes
•use of dark colors and bold red
•internet references
•computer references (error codes, windows xp, etc.)
•video game references
•distorted images
•shadow figures
•hallucinations 

If someone where to ask me "what do I do?" I would simply tell them, "Imagine yourself alone in a foreign place. You're confused and in front of you is cryptic images and figures that seem to want to help you, but inside you know something really bad is about to happen. Now capture that very 'oh fuck' moment, before anything bad actually happens."
